topic: Best local coding LLM: what actually fits 128 GB
title: Best Local Coding LLM: gpt-oss vs GLM
description: What actually fits and flies in 128 GB of unified memory? This local coding LLM comparison climbs three rungs, cost, speed, and fit, for gpt-oss-120b versus GLM-4.5-Air on a 128 GB machine like a DGX Spark or Mac Studio. gpt-oss-120b ships from Ollama as one 65GB MXFP4 download and was measured by the llama.cpp maintainer at 45.34 tokens per second decode, while GLM-4.5-Air's recommended Q4_K_M file is 73.50GB, and the SWE-bench Verified open leaders were never measured on this hardware at all. You'll learn why total parameters decide fit while active parameters decide speed, why a mixture-of-experts model can be huge yet fast, which model to pull tonight, and when to switch. Subscribe to Build Local AI for weekly picks that run on your own hardware. (Narration is AI-generated.)

narration_full: gpt oss or G L M? File size decides. You've got one hundred twenty-eight gigabytes of unified memory, one shared pool, and a coding habit to feed tonight. Unified memory means one pool. Your model weights live in it. So does the K V cache, the scratchpad that grows with every line of context. So does your operating system. The file has to fit with room left over, or nothing runs. Total parameters decide whether it fits. Active parameters decide how fast it thinks. The two numbers pull in opposite directions. It's a mixture of experts, a model that wakes a small slice of itself for each word. All of it sits in your memory. Only the slice does the thinking. Start with cost. Ollama ships gpt oss in exactly one quant, a single sixty-five-gigabyte download, and one command starts it. A quant is just a compression setting, fewer bits per weight. Sixty-five gigabytes leaves real headroom. Now speed, because fitting is not flying. The llama dot cpp maintainer measured this model on this exact class of hardware. It reads back at forty-five point three four tokens a second. That's typing speed, not waiting speed. G L M four point five Air is the other survivor. Its recommended quant, the file the makers suggest, still fits with room to spare, and a richer quant fits too. Its decode speed here? Nobody has measured it on this hardware. What you get instead is more quality per gigabyte of memory. Now the honest catch. On the software engineering benchmark, a board built from real GitHub fixes, the open leaders score far above gpt oss. No page we found has measured them here. Those leaders are full-size models, G L M, Kimi, DeepSeek. Whether any of them fits your box at all, nobody has measured it. pull gpt oss tonight, the measured, one-command pick. Switch to G L M four point five Air when you want more quality per gigabyte of memory. The crown stays in the cloud; the coding stays on your desk.

analogy.vehicle: a big-block engine that fires only a few cylinders per revolution
analogy.mapping: total parameters are the whole engine that must fit the garage (memory); active parameters are the cylinders actually fired each token, which set the speed
analogy.limit: the analogy hides that the whole engine still has to be parked in the garage before any cylinder fires, and that a bigger engine costs nothing per revolution once parked

notes_for_review: The three spoken key numbers are 65GB (cost rung), 45.34 t/s (speed rung), and 73.50GB (GLM fit rung); 128 GB is treated as the premise, and the SWE-bench gap is admitted qualitatively ('the gap is not close') to stay inside the three-number budget, so a reviewer may swap in 26.00 versus 75.80 if digits are preferred. TEACHES lands in scene s3 (total versus active parameters and mixture of experts, each defined in the same breath); EQUIPS lands in scene s8 (the repeatable pull-or-switch rule). GLM-4.5-Air's parameter counts are never claimed because the brief marks them unverified, and its decode speed and the leaders' local fit are stated only as absences.
